questions.question: Which of the following is the safest way to manage a mutex lock in C++ to prevent deadlocks when an exception is thrown?
questions.explanation: `std::lock_guard` uses RAII to automatically unlock the mutex when it goes out of scope, including during exception-driven stack unwinding, avoiding a stuck lock.

questions.question: What is the Curiously Recurring Template Pattern (CRTP) primarily used for in C++?

options.A: Dynamic polymorphism and runtime type checking
options.B: Static polymorphism and avoiding virtual function call overhead
options.C: Preventing memory leaks in circular dependencies
options.D: Enabling garbage collection for specific class hierarchies

questions.explanation: CRTP lets a base class be templated on its derived class, enabling compile-time (static) polymorphism and avoiding the runtime overhead of virtual function calls.

questions.question: In C++11 and later, what does the 'mutable' keyword do when applied to a lambda expression?

options.A: It allows the lambda to modify variables captured by value.
options.B: It forces the lambda to capture all variables by reference.
options.C: It prevents the lambda from being copied.
options.D: It allows the lambda to execute asynchronously.

questions.explanation: By default, a lambda's by-value captures are read-only inside the body. Marking the lambda `mutable` allows it to modify those captured-by-value variables.

questions.question: Which C++ cast should be used to safely cast down a class hierarchy (from a base pointer to a derived pointer) and returns nullptr on failure?
questions.explanation: `dynamic_cast` performs a runtime-checked downcast and returns `nullptr` (for pointers) if the object isn't actually of the target type, unlike `static_cast` which performs no such check.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of using std::optional (introduced in C++17)?

options.A: It automatically initializes pointers to nullptr.
options.B: It provides a type-safe way to represent a value that may or may not be present, avoiding magic values like -1.
options.C: It improves the performance of standard library containers by skipping empty elements.
options.D: It allows multiple inheritance without the diamond problem.

questions.explanation: `std::optional<T>` explicitly represents 'a value or nothing' at the type level, replacing error-prone conventions like returning `-1` or a null pointer to signal absence.

questions.question: When defining a template class, why is it common practice to put the implementation in the header file instead of a .cpp file?

options.A: Templates cannot be compiled into object files because the compiler needs to see the definition to instantiate it for specific types.
options.B: The C++ standard explicitly forbids using .cpp files for templates.
options.C: It speeds up the compilation process by avoiding linking steps.
options.D: Header files have fewer strict syntax rules than .cpp files.

questions.explanation: Templates are instantiated per concrete type at compile time, so the compiler needs to see the full definition wherever the template is used — keeping it in the header makes that possible.

questions.question: What happens if a std::unique_ptr is passed by value to a function?

options.A: The pointer is copied, and both point to the same memory.
options.B: The program will not compile because std::unique_ptr deleted its copy constructor.
options.C: The ownership is temporarily shared until the function returns.

questions.explanation: `std::unique_ptr` has its copy constructor deleted to enforce single ownership, so passing it by value fails to compile; it must be moved or passed by reference instead.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'noexcept' specifier?

options.A: It disables all exception handling in the entire program.
options.B: It tells the compiler that the function does not throw exceptions, allowing for specific optimizations (like in std::vector reallocation).
options.C: It catches any unhandled exceptions and terminates the program silently.
options.D: It forces the function to return an error code instead of throwing.

questions.explanation: `noexcept` tells the compiler a function guarantees it won't throw, which enables optimizations such as `std::vector` using moves instead of copies during reallocation.
